units.translation: But from the oracles what good report is sent to mortals?
by the oracles of this man
I pity you for your fate foretold by oracle
Said of an adopted son, noted from Aeschylus in the Florentine Etymologicum in Miller, Mélanges de littérature grecque, p. 147

Thus Weil restored the defective words κρατοῦσα τοὺς ξένους [the mistress of the house, the strangers], thus Victorius for σκυθρωπὸν [gloomy], and what follows. For thus must be corrected what is written in M: θέτο σκυθρωπόν [she put on a gloomy look], which Erfurdt thought should be written θετοσκυθρωπὸν [feigned-gloomy], an adjective compounded with little probability, i.e. hiding laughter within her eyes, feigning signs of adoptive gloom.

προσποιητός παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ [feigned in Aeschylus]. τίθημι θήσω θετός [I place, I will place, placed]. These words, with the omission of παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ [in Aeschylus], are also read in the Vossian codex of the Etymologicum. In Etym. M. p. 448, 21, with the words παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ [in Aeschylus] likewise omitted, is read θετὸς υἱός: προσποιητός [adopted son: feigned] · τοὺς γὰρ εἰσποιητοὺς καὶ θετοὺς ἔλεγον καὶ θέτην τὸν εἰσποιησάμενον παῖδας θετούς [for they called adopted sons both eispoietoi and thetoi, and thetes the one who adopted children as thetoi]. It is strange that προσποιητός [feigned] is used for εἰσποιητός [adopted], the usual word in this matter, which Larcher wanted to restore in place of προσποιητός [feigned]. Perhaps therefore there were two older glosses, one, to be referred to line 378 of the Choephori, θετός: προσποιητός παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ [thetos: feigned in Aeschylus], the other θετὸς υἱός: εἰσποιητός [adopted son: adopted] · τοὺς γὰρ εἰσποιητούς [for the adopted] etc. Which is the usual meaning of the word θετός [thetos]. But of the former meaning, feigned or pretended, we know no examples except the line of the Choephori, so that the grammarian did a worthwhile thing when he noted it from Aeschylus.

The woman who rules the house bids Aegisthus to call the strangers who have just arrived as quickly as possible, so that he may come and learn more clearly this newly announced report, man from man; to the servants she hides laughter within her eyes, feigning a gloomy look.

ship on which the theori sail
Theoroi or Isthmiastai was the title of a play by Aeschylus (fr. 73-76).

In M θήγει [he sharpens]. Hermann corrected it from the gloss of Hesychius θηγάνει: ὀξύνει [he sharpens: he whets].
